registry_note: Stable source registry through S106. S057-S072 are the focused periodization, calibration, interval-design, taper, and transition addendum researched on 2026-11-11. S073-S106 are a targeted air-travel and time-zone review verified on 2026-11-22: identity checked against PubMed or the official page, full text read for S080, S096, and S100, abstracts otherwise. Access level and applicability limits are explicit.

sources.citation: Buist I, Bredeweg SW, Bessem B, et al. No effect of a graded training program on the number of running-related injuries in novice runners. Am J Sports Med. 2008;36(1):33-39.
sources.title: No effect of a graded training program on the number of running-related injuries in novice runners
sources.population_or_scope: 532 novice recreational runners; 13-week 10% progression versus 8-week standard program
sources.notes: Injury incidence was similar; does not validate a universal progression rate.

sources.citation: Fredette A, Roy JS, Perreault K, Dupuis F, Napier C, Esculier JF. The Association Between Running Injuries and Training Parameters: A Systematic Review. J Athl Train. 2022;57(7):650-671.
sources.title: The Association Between Running Injuries and Training Parameters: A Systematic Review
sources.population_or_scope: 36 prospective studies; 23,047 novice, recreational, and competitive runners
sources.notes: Associations between injury and distance, duration, frequency, intensity, or changes were conflicting.

sources.citation: Frandsen JSB, Hulme A, Parner ET, et al. How much running is too much? Identifying high-risk running sessions in a 5200-person cohort study. Br J Sports Med. 2025;59(17):1203-1210.
sources.title: How much running is too much? Identifying high-risk running sessions in a 5200-person cohort study
sources.population_or_scope: 5,205 adult runners; 588,071 Garmin-recorded sessions over 18 months
sources.notes: Single-session distance spikes were associated with overuse injury; observational and not a validated safe cutoff or PTT-specific rule.

sources.citation: Impellizzeri FM, Tenan MS, Kempton T, Novak A, Coutts AJ. Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio: Conceptual Issues and Fundamental Pitfalls. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2020;15(6):907-913.
sources.title: Acute:Chronic Workload Ratio: Conceptual Issues and Fundamental Pitfalls
sources.population_or_scope: Conceptual and statistical analysis of ACWR use
sources.notes: No causal evidence supports manipulating ACWR to reduce injury; ratio can create artifacts.

sources.citation: Cloosterman KLA, de Vos RJ, Willemsen S, et al. Association Between Global Positioning System-Based Training Load and Injury Risk in Recreational Runners: A Large Prospective Study. J Athl Train. 2026;61(5):341-347.
sources.title: Association Between Global Positioning System-Based Training Load and Injury Risk in Recreational Runners: A Large Prospective Study
sources.population_or_scope: 461 adult recreational runners; 20,425 GPS sessions
sources.notes: Small ACWR-duration association disappeared after excluding baseline injury; authors questioned clinical relevance.

sources.citation: Schwellnus M, et al. International Olympic Committee consensus statement on acute respiratory illness in athletes part 1: acute respiratory infections. Br J Sports Med. 2022.
sources.title: International Olympic Committee consensus statement on acute respiratory illness in athletes part 1: acute respiratory infections
sources.population_or_scope: Athletes with acute respiratory infection
sources.notes: Provides severity assessment, exercise challenge, monitoring, and return-to-sport guidance; clinical consensus rather than a universal training formula.

sources.citation: Snyders C, Pyne DB, Sewry N, Hull JH, Kaulback K, Schwellnus M. Acute respiratory illness and return to sport: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med. 2022;56(4):223-231.
sources.title: Acute respiratory illness and return to sport: a systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.population_or_scope: 54 studies; 31,065 athletes or military recruits
sources.notes: Mean symptom duration about 7 days; return-to-sport data limited and heterogeneous.

sources.citation: Jooste M, Sewry N, Valtonen M, Dyer M, Jordaan E, Schwellnus M. Factors associated with return-to-sport outcomes following pathogen-confirmed acute respiratory infections in athletes: AWARE X study. Br J Sports Med. 2026;60(14):1028-1035.
sources.title: Factors associated with return-to-sport outcomes following pathogen-confirmed acute respiratory infections in athletes: AWARE X study
sources.population_or_scope: 114 pathogen-confirmed acute respiratory infection cases in athletic people
sources.notes: Median return to training, full training, and full performance differed; severity and pathogen mattered.

sources.citation: Muñoz I, Seiler S, Bautista J, et al. Does polarized training improve performance in recreational runners? Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2014;9(2):265-272.
sources.title: Does polarized training improve performance in recreational runners?
sources.population_or_scope: 30 recreational runners; 10-week polarized versus between-threshold training
sources.notes: Both groups improved; primary between-group difference was not statistically significant.

sources.citation: Rosenblat MA, Watt JA, Arnold JI, et al. Which Training Intensity Distribution Intervention will Produce the Greatest Improvements in Maximal Oxygen Uptake and Time-Trial Performance in Endurance Athletes? Sports Med. 2025;55(3):655-673.

sources.source_type: systematic review and individual-participant network meta-analysis

sources.notes: No overall polarized-versus-pyramidal difference; subgroup suggests recreational athletes may respond at least as well to pyramidal training.

sources.citation: Oliveira PS, Boppre G, Fonseca H. Comparison of Polarized Versus Other Types of Endurance Training Intensity Distribution on Athletes' Endurance Performance. Sports Med. 2024;54(8):2071-2095.
sources.title: Comparison of Polarized Versus Other Types of Endurance Training Intensity Distribution on Athletes' Endurance Performance
sources.population_or_scope: 17 studies; 437 endurance athletes
sources.notes: Small VO2peak advantage for polarized training, but no clear advantage for time trial, time to exhaustion, or threshold outcomes.

sources.citation: Seiler KS, Kjerland GO. Quantifying training intensity distribution in elite endurance athletes: is there evidence for an optimal distribution? Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2006;16(1):49-56.
sources.title: Quantifying training intensity distribution in elite endurance athletes: is there evidence for an optimal distribution?
sources.population_or_scope: 11 elite junior cross-country skiers
sources.notes: Seminal observational paper; illustrates that session-goal and time-in-zone methods answer different questions.

sources.citation: Filipas L, et al. Quantifying the Training-Intensity Distribution in Middle-Distance Runners: The Influence of Different Methods of Training-Intensity Quantification. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2019.
sources.title: Quantifying the Training-Intensity Distribution in Middle-Distance Runners: The Influence of Different Methods of Training-Intensity Quantification
sources.population_or_scope: Highly trained middle-distance runners
sources.notes: Heart rate, running speed, and session-RPE methods produced materially different distributions.

sources.citation: Sitko S, Artetxe X, Bonnevie-Svendsen M, et al. What Is Zone 2 Training? Experts' Viewpoint on Definition, Training Methods, and Expected Adaptations. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2025;20(11):1614-1617.
sources.title: What Is Zone 2 Training? Experts' Viewpoint on Definition, Training Methods, and Expected Adaptations
sources.population_or_scope: Expert panel; not a comparative intervention
sources.notes: Preferred definition is immediately below first lactate/ventilatory threshold; adaptations are not unique to a narrow zone.

sources.citation: Tønnessen E, Sandbakk Ø, Sandbakk SB, Seiler S, Haugen T. Training Session Models in Endurance Sports: A Norwegian Perspective on Best Practice Recommendations. Sports Med. 2024;54(11):2935-2953.
sources.title: Training Session Models in Endurance Sports: A Norwegian Perspective on Best Practice Recommendations
sources.population_or_scope: Successful Norwegian elite endurance coaches and athlete training logs
sources.notes: Descriptive best practice, not causal evidence for importing elite volume, lactate targets, or double-threshold sessions.

sources.citation: Comparison of acute physiological responses between one long and two short sessions of moderate-intensity training in endurance athletes. Front Physiol. 2024.
sources.title: Comparison of acute physiological responses between one long and two short sessions of moderate-intensity training in endurance athletes
sources.population_or_scope: 14 male elite endurance athletes; 6x10 min versus two 3x10 min sessions separated by 6.5 h
sources.notes: Acute responses only; does not establish long-term superiority of double threshold.

sources.citation: Faelli E, et al. Effects of Two High-intensity Interval Training Concepts in Recreational Runners. Int J Sports Med. 2019.
sources.title: Effects of Two High-intensity Interval Training Concepts in Recreational Runners
sources.population_or_scope: Recreational runners; 8 weeks; 10-20-30 versus 30-30 intervals
sources.notes: Both improved; 10-20-30 produced lower perceived exertion in this study.

sources.citation: Hov H, et al. Effects of three different high-intensity interval training protocols on VO2max and 3000-m performance. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2023.
sources.title: Effects of three different high-intensity interval training protocols on VO2max and 3000-m performance
sources.population_or_scope: 48 well-trained men; 3 interval sessions weekly for 8 weeks
sources.notes: 4x4 min improved VO2max more than very short protocols; dose is much higher than appropriate during a tendon-limited rebuild.

sources.citation: Comparative effects of interval-training formats on VO2max: systematic review and network meta-analysis. BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil. 2025.
sources.title: Comparative effects of high-intensity, sprint-interval, and repeated-sprint training on VO2max
sources.population_or_scope: 51 studies; 1,261 athletes or active participants
sources.notes: All formats improved VO2max; no clear universal winner; populations and doses were heterogeneous.

sources.citation: Fokkema T, et al. Training for a (half-)marathon: Training volume and longest endurance run related to performance and running injuries. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2020;30(9):1692-1704.
sources.title: Training for a (half-)marathon: Training volume and longest endurance run related to performance and running injuries
sources.population_or_scope: 997 recreational half-marathon and marathon participants
sources.notes: Higher volume and longer runs associated with faster performance; no injury association detected; self-report and confounding limit causality.

sources.citation: Doherty C, Keogh A, Davenport J, Lawlor A, Smyth B, Caulfield B. An evaluation of the training determinants of marathon performance: A meta-analysis with meta-regression. J Sci Med Sport. 2020;23(2):182-188.
sources.title: An evaluation of the training determinants of marathon performance: A meta-analysis with meta-regression
sources.population_or_scope: 85 studies; 137 marathon cohorts
sources.notes: Training volume, frequency, and long-run measures correlate with performance; mostly observational data.

sources.citation: White LJ, Dressendorfer RH, Muller SM, Ferguson MA. Effectiveness of cycle cross-training between competitive seasons in female distance runners. J Strength Cond Res. 2003;17(2):319-323.
sources.title: Effectiveness of cycle cross-training between competitive seasons in female distance runners
sources.population_or_scope: 11 collegiate female distance runners; 5 weeks; 50% running replaced by cycling
sources.notes: Some aerobic performance was maintained; sample and duration were very small.

sources.citation: Menges T, Dindorf C, Dully J, Fröhlich M. Cross-training between running and cycling: effects on VO2max and running performance—a systematic review and meta-analysis. Front Sports Act Living. 2026;8:1843803.
sources.title: Cross-training between running and cycling: effects on VO2max and running performance—a systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.population_or_scope: 7 randomized trials; trained or recreationally active people
sources.notes: No clear between-group differences; wide confidence intervals and old heterogeneous protocols do not prove interchangeability.

sources.citation: Schumann M, Feuerbacher JF, Sünkeler M, et al. Compatibility of Concurrent Aerobic and Strength Training for Skeletal Muscle Size and Function: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Med. 2022;52(3):601-612.
sources.title: Compatibility of Concurrent Aerobic and Strength Training for Skeletal Muscle Size and Function
sources.population_or_scope: 43 studies in healthy adults
sources.notes: No meaningful attenuation of hypertrophy or maximal strength; small attenuation of explosive strength, especially same-session.

sources.citation: Llanos-Lagos C, Ramirez-Campillo R, Moran J, Sáez de Villarreal E. Effect of Strength Training Programs in Middle- and Long-Distance Runners' Economy at Different Running Speeds. Sports Med. 2024;54(4):895-932.
sources.title: Effect of Strength Training Programs in Middle- and Long-Distance Runners' Economy at Different Running Speeds
sources.population_or_scope: 31 studies; 652 middle- and long-distance runners
sources.notes: High-load, plyometric, and combined training can improve running economy; not evidence of injury prevention.

sources.citation: Wu H, Brooke-Wavell K, Fong DTP, Paquette MR, Blagrove RC. Do Exercise-Based Prevention Programs Reduce Injury in Endurance Runners? Sports Med. 2024;54(5):1249-1267.
sources.title: Do Exercise-Based Prevention Programs Reduce Injury in Endurance Runners?
sources.population_or_scope: 9 randomized articles; 1,904 endurance runners
sources.notes: No significant pooled injury reduction; supervised-only post hoc analysis favored intervention; seven studies low quality.

sources.citation: Leppänen M, Viiala J, Kaikkonen P, et al. Hip and core exercise programme prevents running-related overuse injuries in adult novice recreational runners: a three-arm randomised controlled trial. Br J Sports Med. 2024;58(13):722-732.
sources.title: Hip and core exercise programme prevents running-related overuse injuries in adult novice recreational runners
sources.population_or_scope: 325 novice recreational runners; 24 weeks
sources.notes: Supervised hip/core program reduced injury versus static stretching; ankle/foot program did not and had more acute injuries. One population-specific trial.

sources.citation: Ross MH, Smith MD, Mellor R, Vicenzino B. Exercise for posterior tibial tendon dysfunction: a systematic review of randomised clinical trials and clinical guidelines. BMJ Open Sport Exerc Med. 2018;4(1):e000430.
sources.title: Exercise for posterior tibial tendon dysfunction
sources.population_or_scope: 3 trials; 93 adults with diagnosed PTT dysfunction/tendinopathy
sources.notes: Sparse evidence; moderate effects for eccentric strengthening with orthoses/stretching, but dose reporting poor.

sources.citation: Kulig K, Reischl SF, Pomrantz AB, et al. Nonsurgical management of posterior tibial tendon dysfunction with orthoses and resistive exercise: a randomized controlled trial. Phys Ther. 2009;89(1):26-37.
sources.title: Nonsurgical management of posterior tibial tendon dysfunction with orthoses and resistive exercise
sources.population_or_scope: 36 adults with stage I or II diagnosed posterior tibial tendinopathy; 12 weeks
sources.notes: All groups improved; eccentric group improved most; orthoses and stretching were co-interventions; not a runner return-to-run trial.

sources.citation: Houck J, Neville C, Tome J, et al. Randomized Controlled Trial Comparing Orthosis Augmented by Either Stretching or Stretching and Strengthening for Stage II Tibialis Posterior Tendon Dysfunction. Foot Ankle Int. 2015.
sources.title: Randomized Controlled Trial Comparing Orthosis Augmented by Either Stretching or Stretching and Strengthening for Stage II Tibialis Posterior Tendon Dysfunction
sources.population_or_scope: 39 patients with stage II diagnosed PTT dysfunction; 12 weeks

sources.title: Effect of resistance exercise dose components for tendinopathy management
sources.population_or_scope: 110 studies; 3,953 participants across five tendon locations; no PTT studies
sources.notes: Higher external load and lower-than-daily frequency showed favorable patterns; direct PTT extrapolation is not validated.

sources.citation: Myerson MS, Thordarson DB, Johnson JE, et al. Classification and Nomenclature: Progressive Collapsing Foot Deformity. Foot Ankle Int. 2020;41(10):1271-1276.
sources.title: Classification and Nomenclature: Progressive Collapsing Foot Deformity
sources.population_or_scope: Foot and ankle specialist consensus
sources.notes: PCFD is a complex three-dimensional deformity; the term should not be conflated with unassessed medial ankle symptoms.

sources.citation: Gómez-Jurado I, et al. Orthotic treatment for stage I and II posterior tibial tendon dysfunction (flat foot): A systematic review. Clin Rehabil. 2021.
sources.title: Orthotic treatment for stage I and II posterior tibial tendon dysfunction (flat foot)
sources.population_or_scope: 4 randomized trials; 186 diagnosed stage I/II PTTD patients
sources.notes: Orthoses may reduce early-stage pain; personalized arch support sometimes outperformed flat insoles; risk of bias and heterogeneity remain.

sources.citation: Silbernagel KG, Thomeé R, Eriksson BI, Karlsson J. Continued sports activity, using a pain-monitoring model, during rehabilitation in patients with Achilles tendinopathy. Am J Sports Med. 2007.
sources.title: Continued sports activity, using a pain-monitoring model, during rehabilitation in patients with Achilles tendinopathy
sources.population_or_scope: 38 patients with Achilles tendinopathy
sources.notes: Supports monitored continued activity in Achilles rehab; numeric criteria are not validated PTT rules.

sources.citation: Clifford C, Challoumas D, Paul L, Syme G, Millar NL. Effectiveness of isometric exercise in the management of tendinopathy. BMJ Open Sport Exerc Med. 2020;6(1):e000760.
sources.title: Effectiveness of isometric exercise in the management of tendinopathy
sources.population_or_scope: Randomized trials in non-PTT tendinopathies
sources.notes: Isometrics were not consistently superior to isotonic exercise; short-term pain response varied.

sources.citation: Intrinsic-foot-muscle exercise systematic review, 2026. Effects of Intrinsic Foot Muscle-Targeted Exercise Programs on Functional, Neuromuscular, and Biomechanical Outcomes Relevant to Lower-Limb Injury. Sports. 2026;14(10):455.
sources.title: Effects of Intrinsic Foot Muscle-Targeted Exercise Programs on Functional, Neuromuscular, and Biomechanical Outcomes Relevant to Lower-Limb Injury
sources.population_or_scope: 13 randomized-trial reports; 462 participants across mixed lower-limb conditions and healthy groups

sources.citation: Walsh NP, Halson SL, Sargent C, et al. Sleep and the athlete: narrative review and 2021 expert consensus recommendations. Br J Sports Med. 2021.
sources.title: Sleep and the athlete: narrative review and 2021 expert consensus recommendations
sources.population_or_scope: Athletes across sports
sources.notes: A full night or more without sleep impairs performance; effects of 1-3 nights of partial restriction are less certain; individualized needs matter.

sources.citation: Craven J, McCartney D, Desbrow B, et al. Effects of acute sleep loss on physical performance: a systematic and meta-analytical review. Sports Med. 2022/2023.
sources.title: Effects of acute sleep loss on physical performance
sources.population_or_scope: Experimental sleep-loss studies across exercise modes

sources.citation: Manresa-Rocamora A, Sarabia JM, Javaloyes A, Flatt AA, Moya-Ramón M. Heart Rate Variability-Guided Training for Enhancing Cardiac-Vagal Modulation, Aerobic Fitness, and Endurance Performance. Int J Environ Res Public Health. 2021;18(19):10299.

sources.population_or_scope: Endurance-training trials using HRV guidance

sources.citation: Vesterinen V, Nummela A, Heikura I, et al. Individual Endurance Training Prescription with Heart Rate Variability. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016.
sources.title: Individual Endurance Training Prescription with Heart Rate Variability
sources.population_or_scope: 40 recreational endurance runners; 8-week intensive phase after 4-week preparation

sources.citation: Figueiredo DH, Figueiredo DH, Bellenger C, Machado FA. Individually guided training prescription by HRV and self-reported stress tolerance in recreational runners. J Sports Sci. 2022;40(24):2732-2740.
sources.title: Individually guided training prescription by heart rate variability and self-reported measure of stress tolerance in recreational runners
sources.population_or_scope: 36 male recreational runners; 5 weeks
sources.notes: Subjective-guided arm improved more in this small trial; tiny groups and short duration limit confidence.

sources.citation: Performance and Physiological Effects of Race Pace-Based Versus Heart Rate Variability-Guided Training Prescription in Runners. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2025.
sources.title: Performance and Physiological Effects of Race Pace-Based Versus Heart Rate Variability-Guided Training Prescription in Runners
sources.population_or_scope: 28 recreational runners; 6 weeks
sources.notes: No group-by-time interaction; all approaches improved different outcomes. Too small for a universal HRV gate.

sources.citation: Readiness for Training in Athletes: A Systematic Review. 2026.
sources.title: Readiness for Training in Athletes: A Systematic Review
sources.population_or_scope: 14 athlete-monitoring studies
sources.notes: Definitions and measures were inconsistent; predictive ability was limited; combined subjective/objective monitoring was common.

sources.citation: Howard J, Ellis R, Fortner CK, Doyle JA, Otis J. Validity of the Garmin Forerunner 265 to predict VO2max and race performance times. J Med Eng Technol. 2026:1-12.

sources.citation: Miller DJ, Sargent C, Roach GD. A Validation of Six Wearable Devices for Estimating Sleep, Heart Rate and Heart Rate Variability in Healthy Adults. Sensors. 2022;22(16):6317.

sources.citation: Dial MB, Hollander ME, Vatne EA, et al. Validation of nocturnal resting heart rate and heart rate variability in consumer wearables. Physiol Rep. 2025;13(16):e70527.
sources.title: Validation of nocturnal resting heart rate and heart rate variability in consumer wearables

sources.citation: Støve MP, Haucke E, Nymann ML, Sigurdsson T, Larsen BT. Accuracy of the Garmin Forerunner 235 for the assessment of heart rate during rest and activity. J Sports Sci. 2019;37(8):895-901.
sources.title: Accuracy of the Garmin Forerunner 235 for the assessment of heart rate during rest and activity
sources.population_or_scope: 29 adults; rest, cycling, walking, treadmill running, arm movement

sources.citation: Garmin. What Is the Training Readiness Feature on My Garmin Device? Support documentation.
sources.title: Garmin Training Readiness support documentation
sources.population_or_scope: Compatible Garmin devices
sources.notes: Used only to document claimed inputs and behavior, not as independent evidence that the score improves coaching decisions.

sources.citation: Haddad M, Stylianides G, Djaoui L, Dellal A, Chamari K. Session-RPE Method for Training Load Monitoring. Front Neurosci. 2017;11:612.
sources.title: Session-RPE Method for Training Load Monitoring: Validity, Ecological Usefulness, and Influencing Factors
sources.population_or_scope: 36 validation/reliability studies across sports and ages
sources.notes: Session RPE is practical but influenced by environment, fatigue, psychology, and session type; combine with context.

sources.citation: Smyth B, et al. An analysis of internal-external workload decoupling in 82,303 recreational marathon runners. 2022.
sources.title: Internal-external workload decoupling and recreational marathon performance
sources.population_or_scope: 82,303 recreational marathon runners
sources.notes: Decoupling associated with marathon performance; not a validated readiness or injury cutoff for an individual training run.

sources.citation: Environmental heat and humidity effects on heart rate and endurance performance. 2023.
sources.title: Effects of environmental heat and humidity on physiological response and endurance performance
sources.population_or_scope: Endurance exercise under differing temperature/humidity conditions
sources.notes: Heat changes pace-heart-rate relationships and perceived effort; exact transfer depends on protocol and athlete.

sources.citation: Mountjoy M, Ackerman KE, Bailey DM, et al. 2023 IOC consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs). Br J Sports Med. 2023;57(17):1073-1097.

sources.citation: Thomas DT, Erdman KA, Burke LM. American College of Sports Medicine Joint Position Statement: Nutrition and Athletic Performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2016;48(3):543-568.
sources.title: Nutrition and Athletic Performance
sources.population_or_scope: Athletes across sports and training scenarios

sources.title: Longer disciplined tapers improve marathon performance for recreational runners
sources.population_or_scope: More than 158,000 recreational marathon runners with app-recorded training
sources.notes: Associates disciplined multiweek reductions with better marathon outcomes; observational design, selection, and training-history confounding prevent causal individualized rules.

sources.citation: Lipková L, Struhár I, Krajňák J, Puda D, Kumstát M. Field-based tests for determining critical speed among runners and its practical application: a systematic review. Front Sports Act Living. 2025;7:1520914.
sources.title: Field-based tests for determining critical speed among runners and its practical application: a systematic review
sources.population_or_scope: Field-based critical-speed testing protocols in runners
sources.notes: Finds multiple field protocols with high reliability under specified conditions; protocol, mathematical model, test number/order, and environment affect estimates, especially D-prime.

sources.citation: Maffulli N, Padulo J, Oliva F. Noninvasive assessment of the anaerobic threshold in endurance athletes: an evidence-based narrative review of methods, validity, and field feasibility. Br Med Bull. 2026;160(1):ldag037.
sources.title: Noninvasive assessment of the anaerobic threshold in endurance athletes: an evidence-based narrative review of methods, validity, and field feasibility
sources.population_or_scope: Eighty-eight reports comparing noninvasive threshold methods with criterion methods in endurance athletes
sources.notes: Methods may correlate at group level without individual interchangeability; threshold definitions and protocols differ, and agreement/reliability matter more than correlation alone.

sources.citation: Anderson M, Bellenger C, Sabapathy S, Arnold B, Bellinger P. The measurement and application of critical speed and D-prime in running: a scoping review. Sports Med. 2026;56(7):1637-1674.
sources.title: The measurement and application of critical speed and D-prime in running: a scoping review
sources.population_or_scope: Running critical-speed and D-prime protocols, models, performance prediction, and training prescription
sources.notes: Critical speed can support performance modelling and prescription, but protocol/model choices and variable D-prime estimates require transparent method storage and cautious individual use.

sources.citation: Hecksteden A, Pitsch W, Rosenberger F, Meyer T. Repeated testing for the assessment of individual response to exercise training. J Appl Physiol. 2018;124(6):1567-1579.
sources.title: Repeated testing for the assessment of individual response to exercise training
sources.source_type: controlled training trial and methods comparison
sources.population_or_scope: 36 healthy untrained adults; one-year walking/jogging program with repeated VO2max testing
sources.notes: Responder classifications disagreed substantially across methods, illustrating measurement/day-to-day variability and the danger of declaring individual nonresponse from one pre/post comparison.

sources.citation: Bonafiglia JT, Preobrazenski N, Gurd BJ. A systematic review examining the approaches used to estimate interindividual differences in trainability and classify individual responses to exercise training. Front Physiol. 2021;12:665044.
sources.title: A systematic review examining the approaches used to estimate interindividual differences in trainability and classify individual responses to exercise training
sources.population_or_scope: Methods used in exercise-training studies to estimate response heterogeneity and classify responders
sources.notes: Highlights inconsistent analytical approaches and misclassification risk; supports repeated/comparative evidence rather than fixed responder identities.

sources.citation: Buchheit M, Laursen PB. High-intensity interval training, solutions to the programming puzzle: Part I: cardiopulmonary emphasis. Sports Med. 2013;43(5):313-338.
sources.title: High-intensity interval training, solutions to the programming puzzle: Part I: cardiopulmonary emphasis
sources.population_or_scope: High-intensity interval programming variables and acute cardiopulmonary responses across athlete populations
sources.notes: Interval response depends on interacting work, recovery, modality, repetition, and set variables; time near VO2max is only one consideration.

sources.citation: Buchheit M, Laursen PB. High-intensity interval training, solutions to the programming puzzle: Part II: anaerobic energy, neuromuscular load and practical applications. Sports Med. 2013;43(10):927-954.
sources.title: High-intensity interval training, solutions to the programming puzzle: Part II: anaerobic energy, neuromuscular load and practical applications
sources.population_or_scope: High-intensity interval programming, anaerobic contribution, neuromuscular/musculoskeletal load, and periodization
sources.notes: Similar cardiorespiratory sessions can have different anaerobic and mechanical costs; elite example volumes are not recreational prescriptions.

sources.citation: Midgley AW, McNaughton LR. Time at or near VO2max during continuous and intermittent running: a review with special reference to considerations for the optimisation of training protocols to elicit the longest time at or near VO2max. J Sports Med Phys Fitness. 2006;46(1):1-14.
sources.title: Time at or near VO2max during continuous and intermittent running
sources.population_or_scope: Continuous and intermittent running protocols intended to elicit time at or near VO2max
sources.notes: Shows how interval design affects time near VO2max but explicitly notes that multiple adaptations and further experimental evidence should guide competitive-running recommendations.

sources.citation: Barbieri A, Fuk A, Gallo G, et al. Cardiorespiratory and metabolic consequences of detraining in endurance athletes. Front Physiol. 2024;14:1334766.
sources.title: Cardiorespiratory and metabolic consequences of detraining in endurance athletes
sources.population_or_scope: Endurance-trained athletes experiencing short- or long-term training cessation/reduction
sources.notes: Complete or substantial training cessation can reduce cardiorespiratory/metabolic adaptations within weeks; magnitude depends on prior training, duration, and retained stimulus, so no universal loss timetable follows.

sources.citation: Janse van Rensburg et al. Managing Travel Fatigue and Jet Lag in Athletes: A Review and Consensus Statement. Sports Med. 2021.
sources.title: Managing Travel Fatigue and Jet Lag in Athletes: A Review and Consensus Statement
sources.population_or_scope: Athlete travel; circadian physiology; nonpharmacologic and pharmacologic management
sources.notes: Defines travel fatigue versus jet lag; gives direction-dependent adaptation model and practical planning recommendations; repeatedly notes weak athlete evidence.

sources.citation: Janse van Rensburg et al. How to manage travel fatigue and jet lag in athletes? A systematic review of interventions. Br J Sports Med. 2020.
sources.title: How to manage travel fatigue and jet lag in athletes? A systematic review of interventions
sources.population_or_scope: 22 studies; athletes and healthy participants; 14 RCTs; 12 athlete-specific jet-lag studies
sources.notes: Found no eligible travel-fatigue management literature and judged athlete jet-lag intervention evidence low quality.

sources.citation: Botonis et al. Impact of long-haul airline travel on athletic performance and recovery: A critical review of the literature. Exp Physiol. 2025.
sources.title: Impact of long-haul airline travel on athletic performance and recovery: A critical review of the literature
sources.population_or_scope: Athletes or physically active participants crossing at least four zones
sources.notes: Endurance evidence was equivocal and limited to intermittent field tests; strength/power findings varied by test and timing.

sources.citation: Benito et al. Do Long-Haul Travel and Jet Lag Affect Athletes' Physiological, Humoral and Performance Outcomes? A Systematic Narrative Review. Sports (Basel). 2026.
sources.title: Do Long-Haul Travel and Jet Lag Affect Athletes' Physiological, Humoral and Performance Outcomes? A Systematic Narrative Review
sources.population_or_scope: 89 athlete-travel studies across performance, sleep, perceptual, and biological outcomes
sources.notes: Updated evidence map; 49% of studies rated low risk of bias, 17% moderate, and 34% high. Heterogeneity prevents a universal recovery dose.

sources.citation: Rossiter et al. Effects of Long-Haul Travel on Recovery and Performance in Elite Athletes: A Systematic Review. J Strength Cond Res. 2022.
sources.title: Effects of Long-Haul Travel on Recovery and Performance in Elite Athletes: A Systematic Review
sources.population_or_scope: 14 studies, 197 elite athletes, six sports
sources.notes: Only three of ten performance studies reported decrements; sleep, psychometric, and physiological disruption were more common; performance conclusion was inconclusive.

sources.citation: Fowler et al. Greater Effect of East versus West Travel on Jet Lag, Sleep, and Team Sport Performance. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2017.
sources.title: Greater Effect of East versus West Travel on Jet Lag, Sleep, and Team Sport Performance
sources.population_or_scope: 10 physically trained men; 21-hour travel across eight zones Australia–Qatar and return
sources.notes: Eastward return produced worse sleep, fatigue, motivation, and selected intermittent-performance outcomes over the first four days; very small male sample.

sources.citation: Stevens et al. Long-Haul Northeast Travel Disrupts Sleep and Induces Perceived Fatigue in Endurance Athletes. Front Physiol. 2018.
sources.title: Long-Haul Northeast Travel Disrupts Sleep and Induces Perceived Fatigue in Endurance Athletes
sources.population_or_scope: 12 trained masters triathletes; Australia to Hawaii; overnight travel; heat change confounded travel
sources.notes: In-flight sleep fell 4.8 ± 1.2 hours; fatigue increased; sleep and fatigue returned near baseline within about 48 hours; no performance test.

sources.citation: Doherty et al. The impact of long haul travel on the sleep of elite athletes. Neurobiol Sleep Circadian Rhythms. 2023.
sources.title: The impact of long haul travel on the sleep of elite athletes
sources.population_or_scope: Seven elite track cyclists, four women and three men; 21.5-hour trip, seven zones east
sources.notes: Total sleep time fell 268 minutes during travel and 197 minutes on arrival night one (full text, not the abstract); largest disruption occurred in the first 48 hours; no performance endpoint.

sources.citation: Lemmer et al. Jet lag in athletes after eastward and westward time-zone transition. Chronobiol Int. 2002.
sources.title: Jet lag in athletes after eastward and westward time-zone transition
sources.population_or_scope: Top male athletes; six zones west, n=13; eight zones east, n=6
sources.notes: Symptoms persisted approximately five to six days westward and seven days eastward; small nonrandomized groups and sparse testing days.

sources.citation: Wright et al. Effects of travel across time zones (jet-lag) on exercise capacity and performance. Aviat Space Environ Med. 1983.
sources.title: Effects of travel across time zones (jet-lag) on exercise capacity and performance
sources.population_or_scope: 81 healthy male soldiers; six-zone eastward travel
sources.notes: Symptoms mostly diminished by day five; 2.8-km running was slower on days two to three and sprint performance on days one to four, while treadmill RPE/cardiorespiratory function were unchanged.

sources.citation: Fullagar et al. Sleep, Travel, and Recovery Responses of National Footballers During and After Long-Haul International Air Travel. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2016.
sources.title: Sleep, Travel, and Recovery Responses of National Footballers During and After Long-Haul International Air Travel
sources.population_or_scope: 15 elite male footballers; 18 hours predominantly westward; four-zone delay
sources.notes: Travel sleep was curtailed, followed by arrival-night rebound; perceived recovery was largely preserved; westward direction and only four zones limit generalization.

sources.citation: Fowler et al. Effects of simulated domestic and international air travel on sleep, performance, and recovery for team sports. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2015.
sources.title: Effects of simulated domestic and international air travel on sleep, performance, and recovery for team sports
sources.population_or_scope: 10 active men; simulated five-hour domestic versus 24-hour international travel
sources.notes: Five-hour simulation had little effect; 24-hour simulation reduced sleep and next-afternoon intermittent performance and worsened mood/effort. Simulation omitted many real-flight factors.

sources.citation: Stergiopoulos et al. Effects of Simulated Short-Haul Flights on Sport-Specific Performance, Sleep, and Psychophysiological Responses in Football Players. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2025.
sources.title: Effects of Simulated Short-Haul Flights on Sport-Specific Performance, Sleep, and Psychophysiological Responses in Football Players
sources.population_or_scope: 19 highly trained male footballers; two- and four-hour early-morning simulated flights plus control
sources.notes: Next-day repeated sprint, 10-m sprint, jump, and football-test outcomes worsened, alongside preflight-night sleep loss; cannot separate early wake from sitting/restriction.

sources.citation: McGuckin et al. The effects of air travel on performance measures of elite Australian rugby league players. Eur J Sport Sci. 2014.
sources.title: The effects of air travel on performance measures of elite Australian rugby league players
sources.population_or_scope: 12 elite rugby league players; domestic short-haul travel without meaningful time-zone change
sources.notes: Sleepiness and leg tiredness increased but measured strength/power did not clearly worsen; small sample and match context.

sources.citation: Fowler et al. Effects of domestic air travel on technical and tactical performance and recovery in soccer. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2014.
sources.title: Effects of domestic air travel on technical and tactical performance and recovery in soccer
sources.population_or_scope: Six professional male footballers across 12 domestic matches
sources.notes: In-flight oxygen saturation fell; sleep, hydration, fatigue, and recovery findings were equivocal; game and schedule confounding was substantial.

sources.citation: Uchiyama et al. Immediate Effects of Overnight Long-Haul Travel on Physical and Cognitive Performance and Sleep in Professional Male Rugby Union Players (a 2-Part Study). Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2025.
sources.title: Immediate Effects of Overnight Long-Haul Travel on Physical and Cognitive Performance and Sleep in Professional Male Rugby Union Players (a 2-Part Study)
sources.population_or_scope: Professional male rugby union players; n=24 in one component; overnight long-haul travel
sources.notes: Travel sleep fell 219–334 minutes; reactive jump was about 7% lower on arrival day one and still lower on day three; authors recommend more than three days before a match, not tested for running.

sources.citation: Varesco et al. Timing-based strategies to minimize the impact of long-haul travel on sleep: A pilot study in elite athletes traveling for competition. Physiol Rep. 2025.
sources.title: Timing-based strategies to minimize the impact of long-haul travel on sleep: A pilot study in elite athletes traveling for competition
sources.population_or_scope: 10 national speed skaters; 13-zone trip Canada to Beijing; individualized sleep/light/training timing
sources.notes: Sleep was broadly maintained and race rank was unchanged, but no concurrent control or circadian phase marker makes causal attribution impossible.

sources.citation: Lowden and Åkerstedt. Retaining home-base sleep hours to prevent jet lag in connection with a westward flight across nine time zones. Chronobiol Int. 1998.
sources.title: Retaining home-base sleep hours to prevent jet lag in connection with a westward flight across nine time zones
sources.population_or_scope: 19 flight attendants; 50-hour Los Angeles layover after nine-zone westward trip
sources.notes: Home-time sleep reduced layover sleepiness/jet-lag symptoms, but provided no post-return benefit, extended wake before first home sleep, and was preferred by only about two-thirds.

sources.citation: Burgess et al. Preflight Adjustment to Eastward Travel: 3 Days of Advancing Sleep with and without Morning Bright Light. J Biol Rhythms. 2003.
sources.title: Preflight Adjustment to Eastward Travel: 3 Days of Advancing Sleep with and without Morning Bright Light
sources.population_or_scope: Healthy adults; three-day preflight sleep advance with bright-light variants
sources.notes: Advancing sleep one hour/day plus morning bright light advanced melatonin phase by roughly two hours; simulated/preflight setting, not athlete performance.

sources.citation: Boulos et al. Light visor treatment for jet lag after westward travel across six time zones. Aviat Space Environ Med. 2002.
sources.title: Light visor treatment for jet lag after westward travel across six time zones
sources.population_or_scope: 20 travelers; Zurich to New York; bright versus dim evening visor light
sources.notes: Bright light produced a larger melatonin phase delay (2.59 versus 1.58 hours) but did not clearly improve sleep, symptoms, or performance.

sources.citation: Youngstedt et al. Human circadian phase-response curves for exercise. J Physiol. 2019.
sources.title: Human circadian phase-response curves for exercise
sources.population_or_scope: 99 aerobically fit adults; one hour of moderate treadmill exercise at eight clock times over three days
sources.notes: Exercise advanced circadian phase around 07:00 and 13:00–16:00 and delayed it around 19:00–22:00; not a travel trial.

sources.citation: Fowler et al. Sleep Hygiene and Light Exposure Can Improve Performance Following Long-Haul Air Travel. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2021.
sources.title: Sleep Hygiene and Light Exposure Can Improve Performance Following Long-Haul Air Travel
sources.population_or_scope: 20 trained men; 21-hour, eight-zone eastward travel; bundled sleep/light intervention
sources.notes: Intervention improved sleep and selected jump/sprint outcomes but not intermittent-sprint performance; small study, bundled treatment, magnitude-based inference.

sources.citation: Morgenthaler et al. Practice Parameters for the Clinical Evaluation and Treatment of Circadian Rhythm Sleep Disorders: An American Academy of Sleep Medicine Report. Sleep. 2007.
sources.title: Practice Parameters for the Clinical Evaluation and Treatment of Circadian Rhythm Sleep Disorders: An American Academy of Sleep Medicine Report
sources.population_or_scope: Clinical circadian rhythm sleep disorders, including jet lag
sources.notes: Home-time sleep for stays of two days or less is an Option based essentially on the Lowden study; not athlete-specific. Medication recommendations are outside this review.

sources.citation: Craven et al. Effects of Acute Sleep Loss on Physical Performance: A Systematic and Meta-Analytical Review. Sports Med. 2022.
sources.title: Effects of Acute Sleep Loss on Physical Performance: A Systematic and Meta-Analytical Review
sources.population_or_scope: 69 publications, 227 outcomes, 959 participants; 89% male; general exercise populations
sources.notes: Mean performance change −7.56% (95% CI −11.9 to −3.13), with very high heterogeneity (I² 98.1%); afternoon testing was more vulnerable.

sources.citation: Coste et al. Hypoxia-induced changes in recovery sleep, core body temperature, urinary 6-sulphatoxymelatonin and free cortisol after a simulated long-duration flight. J Sleep Res. 2009.
sources.title: Hypoxia-induced changes in recovery sleep, core body temperature, urinary 6-sulphatoxymelatonin and free cortisol after a simulated long-duration flight
sources.population_or_scope: 20 healthy young men; eight hours at simulated 8,000 and 12,000 feet
sources.notes: Circadian temperature timing changed at both exposures; recovery-sleep changes occurred mainly at 12,000 feet, above typical commercial-cabin pressure altitude; no exercise performance test.

sources.citation: Geertsema et al. Effect of commercial airline travel on oxygen saturation in athletes. Br J Sports Med. 2008.
sources.title: Effect of commercial airline travel on oxygen saturation in athletes
sources.population_or_scope: 45 national-level athletes and 18 staff across 10 flights
sources.notes: Oxygen saturation fell about 3-4% during flight (the abstract's wording) and recovered after landing; no evidence that this caused next-day performance loss.

sources.citation: Zubac et al. Up in the Air: Evidence of Dehydration Risk and Long-Haul Flight on Athletic Performance. Nutrients. 2020.
sources.title: Up in the Air: Evidence of Dehydration Risk and Long-Haul Flight on Athletic Performance
sources.population_or_scope: Aircraft microclimate, fluid balance, and athlete performance
sources.notes: Plausible dryness/fluid-shift mechanisms exist, but the review found no clear evidence for incidence, magnitude, duration, or performance effect of flight-induced dehydration in athletes.

sources.citation: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Deep Vein Thrombosis and Pulmonary Embolism. CDC Yellow Book (online page dated 2025-04-23). 2025.
sources.title: Deep Vein Thrombosis and Pulmonary Embolism
sources.population_or_scope: Travel-associated venous thromboembolism risk, symptoms, and prevention boundaries
sources.notes: Page dated 2025-04-23. Travel over four hours is commonly used as the risk threshold; absolute symptomatic VTE risk is low, most cases have additional risk factors, and immobility is central.

sources.citation: Racinais et al. Consensus recommendations on training and competing in the heat. Br J Sports Med. 2015.
sources.title: Consensus recommendations on training and competing in the heat
sources.population_or_scope: Athletes training and competing in hot environments
sources.notes: Heat acclimation commonly requires repeated exposure over roughly one to two weeks and is highly individual; requires a separate topic review.

sources.citation: Miller et al. A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Crossover Studies Comparing Physiological, Perceptual and Performance Measures Between Treadmill and Overground Running. Sports Med. 2019.
sources.title: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Crossover Studies Comparing Physiological, Perceptual and Performance Measures Between Treadmill and Overground Running
sources.population_or_scope: 34 crossover studies in healthy runners
sources.notes: Treadmill and overground responses were not interchangeable at all speeds; treadmill endurance performance was lower (SMD −0.50 ± 0.36). Not hotel-treadmill or travel-specific.

sources.citation: Biggins et al. Impact of Long-Haul Travel to International Competition on Sleep and Recovery in Elite Male and Female Soccer Athletes. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2022.
sources.title: Impact of Long-Haul Travel to International Competition on Sleep and Recovery in Elite Male and Female Soccer Athletes
sources.population_or_scope: 41 elite university-level soccer athletes, 21 men and 20 women; seven zones east; 18-day tournament
sources.notes: Sleep remained negatively affected through five precompetition days and symptoms were reported up to 13 days, but recovery/readiness ratings did not significantly change and performance was not tested.

sources.citation: Clements et al. Travel Across More Time Zones Results in Worse Perceived Fatigue and Sleep in National-Team Footballers. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2023.
sources.title: Travel Across More Time Zones Results in Worse Perceived Fatigue and Sleep in National-Team Footballers
sources.population_or_scope: 355 trips by 50 elite national-team footballers
sources.notes: Per-zone associations with worse fatigue and sleep were statistically significant but models explained only 7–18% of variance; nine or more zones were worst on days one and two.

sources.citation: Clements et al. Flight Path and Scheduling Effects on Perceived Jet Lag, Fatigue, and Sleep in Footballers Traveling to and From National Teams. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2023.
sources.title: Flight Path and Scheduling Effects on Perceived Jet Lag, Fatigue, and Sleep in Footballers Traveling to and From National Teams
sources.population_or_scope: 396 flights by 68 national-team footballers
sources.notes: Daytime arrivals had better perceptual responses than early-morning or late-night arrivals; route and return-to-club context mattered; observational associations only.

sources.citation: Graham et al. The Relationship of Travel Demands With Perceived Fatigue, Sleep, and Wellness of Female National Team Footballers. Int J Sports Physiol Perform. 2026.
sources.title: The Relationship of Travel Demands With Perceived Fatigue, Sleep, and Wellness of Female National Team Footballers
sources.population_or_scope: 342 flights by 45 professional female national-team footballers
sources.notes: Larger shifts, eastward direction, evening arrivals, and return trips were associated with poorer responses, but effects were mostly small/trivial and model R² was .001–.10; most measures improved by day two.
